court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma

issues.label: Oklahoma jurisdiction to modify
issues.why: The court must confirm it had subject-matter jurisdiction to modify a Texas paternity/child-support order registered in Oklahoma (UIFSA/UCCJEA considerations).

issues.label: Proper registration of foreign order
issues.why: The court must determine whether the Texas decree was properly registered and enforceable/modifiable in Oklahoma.

issues.label: Continuing exclusive jurisdiction
issues.why: The court must decide whether Texas or Oklahoma had continuing exclusive jurisdiction over child support under UIFSA at the time of modification.

issues.label: Personal jurisdiction over Father
issues.why: The court must ensure it had personal jurisdiction over Father to enter a modified support and fee order.

issues.label: Notice and due process
issues.why: The court must ensure both parties received adequate notice and a meaningful opportunity to be heard on modification and fees.

issues.label: Material change threshold
issues.why: The court must decide whether a substantial and continuing change in circumstances was shown to justify modification (including income change >25%).

issues.label: Effective date of modification
issues.why: The court must determine the permissible start date for increased support and whether any retroactivity is allowed from filing or other date.

issues.label: Father’s notice breach relevance
issues.why: The court must decide legal effect of Father’s failure to give the 7-day income-change notice (sanctions, fees, evidentiary inferences, or equitable relief).

issues.label: Guidelines must be applied
issues.why: The court must apply Oklahoma child support guidelines and only deviate with legally sufficient findings.

issues.label: High-income case method
issues.why: Because combined income exceeds the guideline cap, the court must use the correct approach for above-cap incomes (needs-based/best-interests and proportionality) rather than mechanically applying the cap.

issues.label: Archer v. Archer implications
issues.why: The court must determine whether Archer controls high-income support calculations and what findings are required if not following it.

issues.label: Required findings for deviation
issues.why: If deviating from guideline amount, the court must make required written findings explaining the deviation and why it is in the children’s best interests.

issues.label: Support based on evidence
issues.why: The court must base the support amount on competent evidence of incomes and children’s needs, not on speculation or an unsupported “sounds reasonable” estimate.

issues.label: Reliance on Father’s offer
issues.why: The court must decide whether it is legally permissible to set support solely on Father’s volunteered amount absent an enforceable agreement and required findings.

issues.label: Enforceable agreement requirements
issues.why: If the $2,250 is treated as an agreement, the court must determine whether there was a valid stipulation/meeting of the minds, approved by the court, consistent with the children’s best interests.

issues.label: Children’s reasonable needs
issues.why: The court must determine the children’s reasonable direct and indirect expenses and whether Mother’s claimed budget is credible and properly attributed to the children.

issues.label: Standard of living consideration
issues.why: The court must consider the children’s right to share in a higher standard of living given Father’s substantial income while avoiding impermissible wealth transfer.

issues.label: Mother’s income imputation
issues.why: The court must decide whether to impute additional income to Mother based on alleged earning capacity (law practice) and whether imputation is supported by evidence and proper standards.

issues.label: Father’s income determination
issues.why: The court must determine Father’s gross income accurately (wages, bonuses, commissions, deferred comp, perks) and address job changes and volatility.

issues.label: Combined income calculation
issues.why: The court must compute each parent’s percentage share of combined income for allocation of support obligations even in above-cap cases.

issues.label: Parenting time adjustment
issues.why: The court must consider whether any visitation/overnight adjustment applies given supervised visitation and minimal contact.

issues.label: Health insurance allocation
issues.why: The court must address who provides/paid health insurance and how premiums and uncovered medical expenses are allocated under guidelines.

issues.label: Childcare and education costs
issues.why: The court must consider guideline treatment of work-related childcare, school, extracurricular, and other allowable additions.

issues.label: Other children/support duties
issues.why: The court must consider any other legal dependents or existing support orders affecting either parent’s ability and guideline computations.

issues.label: Tax considerations
issues.why: The court must ensure any tax-related assumptions/benefits (credits, exemptions if applicable) are handled consistently with Oklahoma law and current tax rules.

issues.label: Evidentiary burdens
issues.why: The court must allocate burdens of proof on modification, income, and needs and decide whether the evidence met those burdens.

issues.label: Credibility and lack of knowledge
issues.why: The court must weigh Father’s limited knowledge of children’s expenses and decide what weight to give his testimony versus Mother’s documentation.

issues.label: Discovery compliance and sanctions
issues.why: The court must address whether Father obstructed discovery and whether sanctions (including fee shifting) are warranted under applicable statutes/rules.

issues.label: Attorney-fee authority source
issues.why: The court must identify a statute or agreement authorizing attorney fees/costs in this paternity/child-support modification and apply it correctly.

issues.label: Proper fee standard
issues.why: If authorized, the court must apply the correct criteria (reasonableness, equity, needs/ability to pay, and/or prevailing-party or misconduct standards depending on statute).

issues.label: Segregation of fees rationale
issues.why: The court must explain why only discovery-related fees were awarded if other work was necessary/caused by the case, and whether such limitation is legally permissible.

issues.label: Required findings for fees
issues.why: The court must make sufficient findings to permit appellate review of the fee award basis, amount, and factors considered.

issues.label: Reasonableness of fee amount
issues.why: The court must assess reasonableness using evidence (time records, rates, necessity) and not arbitrariness.

issues.label: Costs recoverability scope
issues.why: The court must determine which litigation expenses qualify as taxable costs versus non-taxable expenses and whether they were properly proven.

issues.label: Equitable considerations for fees
issues.why: The court must consider parties’ relative ability to pay and whether Father’s conduct (non-notice, delay, discovery issues) justifies shifting fees.

issues.label: Settlement-offer relevance
issues.why: The court must decide whether alleged settlement offers affect fee entitlement or amount under any applicable statute/rule.

issues.label: Abuse of discretion review readiness
issues.why: The court must create an order with adequate legal reasoning and factual findings so the appellate court can review for abuse of discretion.

issues.label: Child support order clarity
issues.why: The court must ensure the support order is sufficiently specific (amount, commencement, payment method, arrears, medical allocation) to be enforceable.

issues.label: Potential arrearage calculation
issues.why: If modification is effective earlier than the order date, the court must calculate any arrears and payment schedule consistent with law.

issues.label: Interest and enforcement terms
issues.why: The court must address statutory interest, withholding, and enforcement mechanisms required for support orders.

issues.label: Attorney-fee enforcement
issues.why: The court must specify how fee judgment is enforced and whether it is support-related or a separate judgment affecting collection methods.
